title: The Blaschka Object Network — Cornell Ward Procurement and Custody Retrieval Register
scope: Cornell archival units that can test the chronology of Ward-mediated acquisition and the later custody/restoration history of the Blaschka marine-invertebrate collection. Direct finding-aid evidence is separated from a published secondary claim about individual Ward letters.

records.repository: Cornell University Library, Division of Rare and Manuscript Collections
records.collection: John Henry and Anna Botsford Comstock papers
items: Henry Augustus Ward to John Henry Comstock, 3 October 1885
Henry Augustus Ward to John Henry Comstock, 8 October 1885
Henry Augustus Ward to John Henry Comstock, 23 October 1885
records.finding_aid_evidence: Cornell's official finding aid lists three Henry Augustus Ward letters in Box 2, Folder 7 and identifies Ward as a natural scientist.
records.secondary_content_claim: William Warmus states that the 23 October 1885 Ward-to-Comstock letter refers to a shipment of glass models. He also reports a 16 October 1882 Ward-to-President Andrew D. White letter referring to 'beautiful glass models' of jellyfish/medusae and uses this to argue for an earlier Cornell acquisition layer.
records.guard: The 1885 folder location is primary-catalogue evidence, but the glass-model content claim is secondary until the letter is inspected. The 1882 Ward-to-White letter has not yet been matched to a stable Cornell finding-aid reference in this pass and is therefore a retrieval lead, not a document-level archival citation.
research_questions: Does the 23 October 1885 letter identify a shipment date, quantity, catalogue numbers, price, packing or payment?
Do the 3 and 8 October letters form part of the same order sequence?
Can the reported 16 October 1882 Ward-to-White letter be located in Andrew D. White presidential/personal correspondence and compared with the 1885 sequence?
Was Cornell's collection acquired in more than one Ward-mediated purchase rather than one 1885 event?

research_observation: Cornell is unusually useful because a possible nineteenth-century Ward procurement sequence and multiple twentieth-/twenty-first-century custody, loan, restoration and exhibition files survive in the same institutional archive. This permits a long object biography without treating later collection history as a substitute for the still-unresolved original purchase chronology.
